summary: The manuscript fits the deterministic-equivalent ridge risk to a pilot's LOGO regularisation path (RPM) and benchmarks pilot-based learning-curve forecasts on 38 public NIR/MIR calibration tasks. As a competitor I checked whether simpler rules match or beat the proposed forecaster, whether its advantages come from other factors, and whether the story oversells it. Recomputing from the raw per-pilot results gives the following. (1) RPM's only clear win, against IPL3, is in the level of the error and not in forecasting the curve. RPM predicts about 14% of the actual improvement (implied slope -0.013 vs true -0.065 per doubling). Its 'near-unbiasedness' is an optimistic pilot anchor cancelling an under-predicted gain. In the authors' own gain analysis RPM, IPL3 and FLAT are tied (Holm p = 1.0). (2) A data-free fixed-ratio rule (pilot CV minus 2-9% RMSE per doubling) is significantly better than RPM and RPM-w across the whole plausible range, at every pilot size, and on 25/25 tasks at extrapolations of 16x or more. FLAT is never worse than RPM-w. (3) The pilot CV anchor (minimum of the LOGO path) is optimistically biased by 5-19%, which confounds the rankings and the 'ill-conditioned sample size' conclusion. (4) The slope-noise finding and the recommended 8.3%-per-doubling rule depend on mixing n-ranges and on transfer within the same application family; under leave-family-out transfer SLOPE-T error rises from 0.251 to 0.413. (5) The eigen-spectrum from unlabelled spectra does not change RPM's forecasts, so the 'measured, not assumed' argument does not hold. The theory-validation part (RQ1) holds up: the large-sample fit reproduces curves much better than a one-slope rule (0.113 vs 0.208, which I checked). The paper is candid in many places, but its framing, abstract and recommendation (vi) still oversell RPM, and the evaluation anchor needs fixing.
strengths: A pre-registration and a time-stamped decision log exist, and negative results (RPM-T failure, FLAT parity, failed decision metric) are reported rather than hidden.
The benchmark is large and leakage-controlled (38 tasks, group-disjoint splits, replicate averaging, 2,640 pilots) and includes the no-improvement and transferred-slope rules as competitors.

RQ1 holds up: the large-sample theory fit reproduces ridge and PLS curves (mean |log err| 0.113/0.126) much better than a one-parameter slope rule anchored at the same full-pool CV error. I recomputed the rule: 0.208, better on only 7/38 tasks, Wilcoxon p < 1e-6.
The raw per-pilot outputs are released and complete, so every claim could be recomputed.

issues.title: RPM's headline win over IPL3 and its 'nearly unbiased' status come from the error level, not from forecasting the learning curve
issues.description: The abstract and Section 4.3 lead with RPM cutting the error from 0.429 (IPL3) to 0.284 (better on 35/38 tasks, p<0.0001) and describe RPM as 'nearly unbiased (+0.038)'. The raw results show that RPM forecasts an almost flat curve. Its accuracy at the level of the error comes from two biases that cancel. (a) The pilot path that RPM is fitted to is optimistic: pilot CV is below the truth at n0 by -0.124 log-RMSE on average. (b) RPM predicts only a small fraction of the real improvement (+0.209 gain bias). RPM's signed error (+0.085 for n0>=50) is the sum of these two (-0.124 + 0.209). Once the shared pilot-level error is removed, RPM has no skill over IPL3 or FLAT. The paper's own post-hoc gain analysis gives RPM 0.231, IPL3 0.232 and FLAT 0.245, all Holm p = 1.000. RPM beats IPL3 on only 17 of 38 tasks and loses on 21. The 35/38 headline therefore shows that a nearly flat forecast suffers less than an over-steep one from the optimistic anchor. It does not show that the random-matrix theory extrapolates better. To be fair, RPM's slopes are rank-correlated with the true slopes across tasks (Spearman 0.65), but IPL3's are more so (0.745), and RPM's are compressed about fivefold.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from results/raw_results.csv (scripts in /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R10/a3.py, a11.py). For n0 in {50,100,200}: mean RPM predicted gain log[RPM(n)/pilotCV] = -0.034 vs true gain -0.243, so RPM predicts about 14% of the improvement. Median RPM implied slope between first and last horizon = -0.013 per doubling (IQR -0.026 to -0.006) vs -0.065 for the truth over the same horizons. 60% of pilots have an RPM slope shallower than -0.02 per doubling. Correlation of RPM and FLAT forecasts = 0.96. Task-median RPM slopes range from -0.062 to -0.003, against -0.528 to +0.06 for the truth. Decomposition of RPM signed error: pilot level -0.124 + gain error +0.209 = +0.085. Gain analysis: tables/T14_posthoc_gain_and_decision.md (RPM 0.231, IPL3 0.232, FLAT 0.245) and T14b (RPM vs IPL3: 17 wins, 21 losses, Holm p = 1.0; vs FLAT Holm p = 1.0). Manuscript lines 13, 176 and 281 ('removed most of the optimism').
issues.corrective_action: Report the decomposition error = pilot-level error + gain error for every method in the main text, and make the gain error a co-primary endpoint. Remove 'nearly unbiased' or qualify it as the result of compensating biases. Rewrite the abstract and conclusions so the RPM-vs-IPL3 result is not presented as evidence that the theory forecasts learning curves. On the information a learning-curve forecaster adds, RPM is tied with IPL3 and FLAT. State plainly that RPM under-predicts improvement about fivefold.

issues.title: A data-free fixed-ratio power law dominates RPM and RPM-w, and the recommendation to use RPM-w when no previous calibrations exist (Sec. 4.10 (vi)) is not supported
issues.description: The brief asked whether a fixed-ratio rule or a power law with a sensible prior is as good or better. It is clearly better. Take the pilot CV error and reduce log-RMSE by a fixed s per doubling of n. This uses no theory, no unlabelled spectra and no other data sets. For any s between -0.02 and -0.09 (2-9% per doubling, a range any analyst would accept a priori) it is significantly more accurate than the pre-registered RPM. With s = -0.05 the mean task error is 0.222, against 0.284 for RPM and 0.271 for RPM-w. At extrapolations of 16x or more it is better than RPM-w on 25 of 25 tasks, and it is better at every pilot size. The value -0.05 was chosen in-sample, but the advantage holds over the whole plausible range, so it does not depend on tuning. The zero-parameter FLAT rule is also never worse than RPM-w (0.266 vs 0.271; Wilcoxon p = 0.55; FLAT better on 21/38 tasks). FLAT needs nothing beyond the pilot. Recommendation (vi) presents RPM-w as the tool for the 'no previous calibrations' case and calls it 'far more reliable than curve-shape extrapolation'. In that case FLAT is at least as accurate. FLAT also gets the narrowest calibrated bands (80%: width factor 1.766 vs 2.046 for RPM-w). Without previous calibrations, RPM-w has only its bootstrap bands, which cover 43.7% at nominal 80%.
issues.evidence: Recomputed (a2.py, a9.py). Per-task mean |log err| of pilotCV + s*log2(n/n0) vs pre-registered RPM, two-sided Wilcoxon, raw p: s=-0.02: 0.240 (29/38 better, p=0.003); s=-0.04: 0.224 (31/38, p=0.0002); s=-0.05: 0.222 (30/38, p<0.0001); s=-0.07: 0.227 (31/38, p<0.0001); s=-0.09: 0.245 (25/38, p=0.0014). Against RPM-w (0.271): s=-0.05 is better on 31/38 (p=0.0004). For ratio >=16 (25 tasks): 0.180 vs RPM-w 0.291 (25/25 tasks). By n0 (s=-0.05 vs RPM-w): 25: 0.276 vs 0.347; 50: 0.195 vs 0.241; 100: 0.160 vs 0.211; 200: 0.107 vs 0.159. FLAT vs RPM-w: p = 0.547. Calibrated band widths: tables/T16_posthoc_loso_conformal_bands.md. RPM-w bootstrap coverage 43.7%/59.9%: manuscript line 210. Recommendation (vi): line 269.
issues.corrective_action: Add a fixed-ratio baseline family (pilot CV x 2^(s*log2(n/n0)) over a pre-declared grid of s) to Table 2. Delete recommendation (vi) or replace it with 'use the pilot CV error (FLAT) or a modest fixed improvement'. Change contribution (ii) in the Introduction so that RPM is presented as an analysis tool that explains the identifiability limit, not as a forecaster to recommend.

issues.title: The abstract and conclusions oversell RPM against the simple rules and leave out the pre-registered endpoints that RPM failed
issues.description: The abstract calls FLAT (0.266) and SLOPE-T (0.251) 'equally accurate' to RPM (0.284). SLOPE-T is in fact significantly better than the pre-registered RPM, and FLAT is numerically better. The pre-registered hypothesis H(b)/RQ2 said RPM would beat 'learning-curve extrapolation and simple rules', and it failed against the simple rules. FLAT beats RPM in every pre-specified stratum: every pilot size, the soil family (23 tasks, the only family with long extrapolations), the PLS ground truth, and 6 of 7 robustness scenarios. The abstract does not say that RPM failed the pre-registered uncertainty endpoint E4 (bootstrap coverage 42.3%/58.3% at nominal 80/95%). It does not say that RPM did worst of all curve forecasters except FLAT on the pre-registered decision endpoint E5 (4.7% vs IPL3 25.1% within a factor of two at 4n0). It mentions only the post-hoc calibrated bands. Section 4.3 says that against the PLS truth 'the ordering was unchanged', but the order changes: under ridge truth it is SLOPE-T < FLAT < RPM, under PLS truth FLAT < SLOPE-T < RPM. Under PLS truth FLAT beats RPM on 26/38 tasks (raw p = 0.027, Holm 0.055). PLS is the calibration method chemometricians actually use.
issues.evidence: tables/T3c_posthoc_stats_slopeT_reference.md: SLOPE-T vs RPM 25/13, Holm p = 0.047 (manuscript Table 2: 0.031). tables/T2b_accuracy_by_n0.md, RPM vs FLAT: n0=25 0.373 vs 0.329; 50 0.247 vs 0.236; 100 0.229 vs 0.200; 200 0.164 vs 0.139. tables/T11_accuracy_by_family.md, soil: RPM 0.250 vs FLAT 0.211; mango 0.243 vs 0.167. tables/T4b_stats_pls_truth.md: FLAT vs RPM 12/26, raw p 0.0274, Holm 0.0547. Table 4 (manuscript lines 248-256): FLAT < RPM in raw, SG1, Kennard-Stone, noise, mango i.i.d. and new-population scenarios. RPM is better only under the new-season shift, which the authors themselves call 'compensating biases, not skill'. Pre-registration (supplementary/EXPERIMENT_DESIGN_preregistration.md, RQ2 and hypothesis H(b)); EXPERIMENT_LOG.md 14:40 'Pre-registered decision metric unfavourable to RPM'. Abstract line 13; line 198 ('ordering was unchanged').
issues.corrective_action: Abstract Results: state that the pre-registered hypothesis against simple rules was not supported, that SLOPE-T was significantly better than RPM, that FLAT was numerically better at every pilot size and in the soil family, and that RPM's pre-registered bands under-covered (42%/58%) and its decision accuracy was 4.7%. Correct the 'ordering unchanged' sentence for the PLS truth. Consider recasting the title and the framing of contribution (ii) as a benchmark with a negative result for theory-based extrapolation.

issues.title: The pilot CV error used as anchor, as FLAT and as RPM's fitting target is optimistically biased; this confounds the method rankings and the 'ill-conditioned sample size' conclusion
issues.description: FLAT, the SLOPE-T anchor and the path RPM is fitted to all use the minimum of the pilot's LOGO CV path over 53 penalties (forecasters.flat_forecast; forecast_experiment.run_pilots, pilot_cv = min(path)). The minimum of a CV curve is a known optimistically biased estimate of the error of the tuned model. The raw results confirm this. Pilot CV is below the ground truth at the same calibration size by -0.187, -0.107 and -0.055 log-RMSE at n0 = 50, 100 and 200. After allowing for the Jensen gap between the mean-MSE truth and per-pilot log errors, the residual optimism is still about -0.135, -0.085 and -0.046. This systematic bias is the same size as one or two doublings of the learning curve, and it decides which methods 'win'. Flat or nearly flat forecasts (FLAT, RPM) benefit because the optimistic anchor cancels their pessimism. Steep forecasts (IPL3, and SLOPE-T with the true median slope) are penalised: SLOPE-T bias is -0.093, and the best fixed slope (-0.05) is much shallower than the true median slope (-0.086). The same bias drives the decision-metric failure that Section 4.5 attributes to intrinsic ill-conditioning. In 31.7% of the 4n0 decisions (and 12.8% at 16n0) the pilot CV is already at or below the true RMSE at n* = 4n0. Any anchored method that forecasts improvement then returns n-hat = n0 and fails by construction. That is a correctable systematic error, not only sampling noise.
issues.evidence: Recomputed (a3.py, a4.py, a5.py). Mean of pilot_cv_logrmse - truth_logrmse(n0): n0=50 -0.187 (median -0.165), 100 -0.107, 200 -0.055; task-level median -0.123; the pilot CV is optimistic on 34 of 38 tasks. The only exceptions are three ICRAF-VisNIR tasks (the exploratory data set; +0.03 to +0.05) and Diesel:cn (+0.105). Jensen correction from truth SEs (CV of test MSE at n=50 = 0.39): about 0.035-0.05. Decision check: pilot CV <= truth(4n0) in 31.7% of pilots (n0=25: 34.6%, 50: 37.1%, 100: 29.4%, 200: 22.5%). Manuscript line 214 ('ill-conditioned ... for a structural reason').
issues.corrective_action: Replace the anchor with an estimate of the pilot's current error that is free of selection bias: nested LOGO, or a selection-bias correction such as the Tibshirani & Tibshirani (2009) or bootstrap .632+ type. Re-score FLAT, SLOPE-T, IPL3 and RPM, and re-run the decision metric with it. Also report results against the median realised RMSE as well as sqrt(mean MSE). Revise the 'ill-conditioned' argument in Section 4.5 to separate systematic anchor bias from pilot noise.
issues.proposed_experiment: On the existing 2,640 pilots, which are reproducible from the SHA-256 seeds, compute the nested-LOGO (or selection-bias-corrected) pilot error. Re-run FLAT, SLOPE-T and the fixed-ratio rules with this anchor; re-fit RPM with its prediction at n0 anchored to it; recompute Table 2, the gain analysis and Table S21. This costs about as much as the existing within-pilot curve for IPL3.

issues.title: Claim that RPM exploits spectral structure measured from unlabelled spectra is not supported; under r = 1 RPM is effectively a fixed-shape two-parameter curve
issues.description: Section 2.4 sets RPM apart from empirical curve fitting because the extrapolation 'rests on the unlabelled eigen-spectrum ... this is measured, not assumed', whereas curve fitting 'must assume the shape of the whole curve'. The Introduction says the other approaches do not use 'the structure of spectroscopic data'. The authors' own ablation shows the eigen-spectrum hardly matters. Pilot-only covariance, 250 unlabelled spectra and extra library spectra all change the error by at most +0.011 (n.s.). For RPM-T, the pilot-only covariance is even much better than the pool spectrum (0.258 vs 0.392). With r fixed at 1 the forecast shape is set by the assumed isotropic prior, so RPM is in practice a two-parameter curve with an assumed shape. That is the property Section 2.4 criticises in curve fitting. The forecasts confirm it: RPM's implied slopes cluster near zero for every task (issue 01). The methodological novelty of RPM is therefore weak. The literature matrix (supplementary/LITERATURE_MATRIX_AND_NOVELTY_MAP.md, 'Closest prior art and residual risk') concedes that the ingredients are known and that the contribution may be judged a 'principled combination'. The combination also does not beat trivial rules.
issues.evidence: Table 3 (manuscript lines 221-232): pilot-only covariance 0.254 vs 0.242 (Holm p = 1.000); 250 unlabelled -0.003 (p = 1.000); extra library -0.003 (p = 0.297). Line 235: RPM-T 0.392 vs RPM-T-pilotcov 0.258 (Holm p = 0.0007). Section 2.4 line 82; Introduction line 24; abstract line 11 ('no principled method predicts ...').
issues.corrective_action: Remove or heavily qualify the 'measured, not assumed' argument in Section 2.4 and the claim about using spectroscopic structure. State that with r = 1 the forecast is insensitive to the eigen-spectrum, so unlabelled spectra are not needed. Present RPM as an explanatory model, using the large-sample fits, rather than as a forecasting method that uses spectral structure.

issues.title: The finding that the noise fraction 'governs' the slope is confounded by data-set size and the n-range over which slopes are computed, and depends on 13 small designed or laboratory data sets
issues.description: The abstract ('governed mainly by the irreducible-noise fraction'), Section 4.2 and the Conclusions ('above all by the irreducible-noise fraction') rest on a cross-task correlation. Two problems undermine it. First, slopes are fitted over very different n ranges: 50-100 for Tecator and CGL, 50-200 for Diesel, 50-6400 for KSSL. A learning curve is steepest at small n, so the small data sets have steep slopes because only the early part of their curve was observed. Data-set size (n_pool) correlates with slope more strongly (Spearman 0.62) than the noise fraction does (0.59). Second, the association is carried by the 13 CGL, Tecator and Diesel tasks. Without them, Spearman rho for the noise fraction falls to 0.30 (p = 0.15), and R^2 of slope on log noise fraction falls from 0.675 to 0.072. Within the 23 soil tasks it is a modest 0.45 (p = 0.03). The noise fraction also comes from the large-sample theory fit to the same curve. A curve near its fitted floor is shallow almost by definition, so the relationship is partly circular. The 'median 8.3% per doubling' figure mixes slopes from incompatible n ranges in the same way.
issues.evidence: tables/T17_posthoc_slope_explanation.md: n_pool rho = 0.624 (p = 2.8e-5) vs noise_frac rho = 0.590. Recomputed (a10.py) from results/slope_per_doubling.csv and alignment_exponents.csv: excluding CGL/Tecator/Diesel (n = 25) rho = 0.299, p = 0.146; R^2 (log noise only) 0.675 overall vs 0.072 without those tasks; soil only rho = 0.448, p = 0.032. Table 1 max n per family; tables/T17b_slope_by_region.md (soil MIR -0.084, Vis/NIR -0.079 vs CGL -0.415, Tecator -0.195).
issues.corrective_action: Recompute all slopes over a common n window (e.g. 50-200 for every task, and 100-800 where available). Report partial correlations that control for the n-range or n_pool, and a within-family (soil) analysis. Rephrase the abstract and conclusions ('associated with' rather than 'governed mainly by'), and give the slope median only for comparable windows.

issues.title: The recommended transferred-slope rule only works when the slope comes from the same application family; it fails under leave-one-family-out transfer
issues.description: Practical recommendation (ii) and the abstract recommend the pilot CV error 'combined with a typical slope' of about 8.3% per doubling. The supporting evidence, SLOPE-T, uses leave-one-source-out transfer, but the sources are not independent domains. For a KSSL soil task the prior comes from ICRAF, AfSIS and NeoSpectra soil tasks with the same four analytes (OC, clay, pH, CEC). The LOSO priors cover only -0.084 to -0.099 for all 38 tasks, so SLOPE-T is in effect a single soil-derived constant. Under a stricter leave-one-family-out transfer (soil prior from non-soil tasks and vice versa), SLOPE-T's mean error rises from 0.251 to 0.413. For the 23 soil tasks it rises from 0.208 to 0.475 (bias -0.467), which is worse than IPL3 overall (0.429). A user with a genuinely new application cannot know which 'typical slope' applies. The limitation sentence that the rule 'needs prospective validation' understates this. Because of the optimistic anchor (issue 04), the 8.3% figure is also miscalibrated for the pilot CV error that practitioners compute: SLOPE-T bias is -0.093, and a 5% per doubling rule is more accurate (0.222 vs 0.251).
issues.evidence: Recomputed (a12.py): median slope soil -0.081 vs non-soil -0.195. Leave-family-out SLOPE-T: overall 0.413; soil 0.475 (bias -0.467); non-soil 0.316. results/slope_per_doubling.csv, column slope_loso_prior, range -0.0992 to -0.0844. Manuscript lines 15 and 269 (ii), and Limitation 3 (line 275).
issues.corrective_action: Report leave-one-family-out (or leave-one-domain-out) SLOPE-T alongside LOSO, and state that the slope prior is domain-specific. Qualify recommendation (ii) and the Significance statement so they apply only to settings with comparable earlier calibrations from the same domain. Re-derive the recommended slope for an unbiased anchor (issue 04).

issues.title: Straw-man baselines inflate the 'significantly better than every other curve-shape extrapolation' claim, and IPL3 is configured unfavourably
issues.description: LOG2 is fitted in MSE space as max(a - b log m, 1e-12). 70.8% of its forecasts sit at the hard-coded 1e-12 floor (median signed error -12.85), so its mean error of 10.127 measures the clip constant, not a method. EXP3 hits the floor in 6.9% of forecasts, and 24.5% of its forecasts are more than tenfold too low. DF-OLS plugs a ridge training RSS and tr(H) into an OLS formula, which no chemometric sample-size guidance uses. These four methods enter the Holm family and the text ('significantly more accurate than every other curve-shape extrapolation'), which pads the comparison. IPL3, the one established competitor, is set up permissively: exponent c is allowed up to 3 on the MSE scale, i.e. MSE proportional to m^-3, far beyond the parametric rate of 1; the asymptote a can go to 0; and the within-pilot curve starts at 25% of the pilot (about 6 samples for n0 = 25), where an inner-LOGO-tuned ridge with p of about 200 is erratic and the curve becomes too steep. A power law with a sensible prior (c <= 1, a above a fraction of the pilot CV error, or the fixed-exponent rule of issue 02) was not tested, apart from the post-hoc SLOPE-T.
issues.evidence: Recomputed (a8.py): LOG2 70.8% of rows at the floor 0.5*ln(1e-12), and 71.1% more than tenfold optimistic; EXP3 6.9% at the floor and 24.5% more than tenfold optimistic; IPL3 19.1% of forecasts more than twofold optimistic; median IPL3 implied slope -0.144 per doubling vs truth -0.065. Code: code/src/models/forecasters.py CURVES (IPL3 bounds ([0,0,0.01],[inf,inf,3.0]); LOG2 floor 1e-12), pilot_subsample_curve fracs=(0.25,...,0.85), dfols_forecast. Manuscript line 176.
issues.corrective_action: Drop LOG2, EXP3 and DF-OLS from the confirmatory Holm family, or re-implement them sensibly (e.g. fit on log-RMSE with a floor tied to the data). Report median and trimmed errors next to means. Add a constrained IPL3 (c <= 1, data-informed lower bound on a, sub-curve starting at m >= 20) as the representative power law with a sensible prior.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run the within-pilot curve fits for IPL3 with c in [0.01, 1], a lower bound on a (e.g. >= 0.25 x pilot CV MSE) and fractions starting at max(0.25 n0, 20) on the existing pilots (same seeds). Report it in Table 2 and the gain analysis.

issues.title: The kappa-collapse comparison uses a null that is not like-for-like and exaggerates the support for RPM's structural assumption
issues.description: Section 4.1 says rescaled errors collapse onto kappa with across-n SD 0.041, against 0.519 'for the same errors plotted against the raw penalty'. The two numbers are computed on different sets of points. The collapse statistic uses only penalties with df2/n < 0.8, inside the overlapping kappa window, after the theory prefactor. The reference uses all 53 penalties without the prefactor, including the near-interpolation region where test errors at small n blow up and which was excluded from the collapse statistic. On the same validity region, the raw-penalty null is 0.257. Applying the theory prefactor without the kappa re-mapping already gives 0.079. The kappa mapping itself, the assumption RPM rests on, therefore reduces dispersion from 0.079 to 0.041 (about twofold), not from 0.519 to 0.041 (13-fold).
issues.evidence: code/experiments/analysis.py collapse_dispersion: ref = mean(std(log(ridge_mu_mse[:n_curves]), axis=0)) over all mus, with no validity mask or prefactor. Recomputed (a6.py), medians over 31 tasks: paper collapse 0.041; paper reference 0.519; raw mu, same validity region 0.257; mu axis with prefactor 0.079; kappa axis without prefactor 0.129. Manuscript line 160.
issues.corrective_action: Report like-for-like nulls (same points, same validity mask), and separate the contributions of the prefactor and the kappa mapping. Revise the sentence in Section 4.1 accordingly.

issues.title: Inflated counts and chronology wording
issues.description: (a) 'Table 2 summarises 117,700 forecasts' counts the 11 methods together. Each method has 10,700 pilot x horizon forecasts, and these are strongly correlated within a pilot; the inferential unit is the 38 tasks. (b) Section 3.6 says RPM-w was specified 'after the main run had been executed', but the log shows the main run started at 19:21 and RPM-w was implemented at 19:24-19:27, while the run was executing; the run finished the next day at 14:40. (c) EXPERIMENT_LOG.md lists the 14:55 entry (post-hoc gain analysis added) before the 14:50 entry (RPM-T failure). That ordering makes it hard to confirm that the post-hoc gain analysis was defined independently of the RPM-T results.
issues.evidence: results/raw_results.csv: 10,700 rows per method x 11 = 117,700; numbers.json n_forecast_rows. Manuscript lines 121 and 176; EXPERIMENT_LOG.md rows 19:21, 19:24-19:27, 14:45, 14:55, 14:50, 14:53.
issues.corrective_action: Report forecasts per method and stress that tasks are the unit of inference. Correct the RPM-w timing sentence ('while the main run was executing'). Put the log in chronological order, or explain the out-of-order entry.

recommendation_rationale: No fatal flaw in data handling was found, and the benchmark and the theory-validation results are useful to the field. However, the proposed forecaster is not needed. Its headline advantage over IPL3 disappears once the shared pilot-level error is removed. A one-number fixed-ratio rule, or the zero-parameter FLAT rule, matches or beats it in every stratum. The evaluation anchor is optimistically biased in a way that shapes the rankings. The paper is publishable in ACA only if it is reframed as a benchmark plus identifiability study, with RPM demoted from a recommended forecaster to an explanatory tool. That requires: a de-biased (nested-CV) anchor; fixed-ratio and constrained-power-law baselines; the error decomposition reported for all methods; the slope analysis done over common n windows; leave-family-out transfer results; and an abstract, conclusions and recommendation (vi) rewritten to match. If the authors keep RPM as the central methodological contribution, I would recommend rejection.
